summary: A headshot on the left, then your name, title and company, a thin rule in your brand colour, one contact line and social icons.
bestFor: Most office and client-facing roles
A first signature when you are not sure what you need
Teams that want one safe design for everyone
notes: The contact details sit on a single line separated by pipes, which keeps the signature short. On a narrow phone screen that line wraps rather than overflowing.

summary: Your name in capitals beside a vertical bar in your brand colour, with title, company and contact details stacked underneath.
bestFor: Directors, partners and senior leaders
Finance, law and other formal industries
Anyone who wants a restrained, traditional look
notes: Stacking each contact detail on its own line makes the signature taller but easier to scan, and the vertical bar does the branding without a logo.

summary: A thick brand-colour bar across the top, then your details with P, E and W labels in your brand colour.
bestFor: Larger companies with a strong brand colour
Roles where people mainly call you
Signatures that sit under long, formal emails
notes: The labelled rows tell the reader which number is which at a glance, and the top bar clearly separates the signature from the message above it.

summary: A small headshot beside your name and title, with the company and contact details below, divided by fine horizontal rules.
bestFor: Consultants and account managers
People who reply to long threads
A wide, compact signature that stays short
notes: The photo is smaller than in most templates, so the signature reads as information first and portrait second.

summary: Built around your company logo: logo, name and title, a brand-colour rule, one contact line and social icons.
bestFor: Businesses whose website lookup found a clean logo
Small companies that want the logo seen in every email
Staff who represent the company more than themselves
notes: When a logo is added it takes the company name's place, so the signature does not repeat the business name twice.

summary: Your name in your primary colour, your title in your secondary colour, and a two-colour gradient rule underneath.
bestFor: Brands with two strong colours
Marketing, design and creative roles
Startups that want something less corporate
notes: Outlook for Windows does not render CSS gradients, so the rule falls back to your primary colour there. Everything else in the layout is unchanged.

summary: A brand-colour ring around your headshot and your job title set in a filled brand-colour pill.
bestFor: Sales and business development
Creative and agency roles
Anyone whose job title is the selling point
notes: The pill makes the title the most visible thing after your name, so it suits roles where what you do matters more than where you work.

summary: Headshot, name and company in small capitals, with the contact details in a tinted strip along the bottom.
bestFor: Tech and product companies
Freelancers with a personal brand
People who want a contemporary layout without loud colour
notes: The tinted strip groups every way to reach you in one place, which helps on mobile where the signature is often the only thing visible after a short reply.

summary: No photo: name and title on one line, contact details on the next, then small social icons.
bestFor: Internal email and quick replies
People who prefer not to use a headshot
Very short signatures for busy threads
notes: It is one of the lightest templates, which keeps long reply chains readable when every message repeats the signature.

summary: Plain text only: your name, title, company and contact details stacked line by line, with social links written as words.
bestFor: Organisations that block images in email
Accessibility-first and plain-text users
Academics, government and legal teams
notes: There are no images at all, so nothing can be blocked, stripped or flagged. It is the most predictable template across every email client.

summary: A thin vertical line in your brand colour beside stacked text details, with no photo.
bestFor: Minimal personal brands
Writers, editors and researchers
A quiet signature that still carries your colour
notes: The single line is the only decoration, which gives a hint of brand colour without a logo or headshot.

summary: A headshot and your details with larger social icons, so your profiles get more attention than in a standard layout.
bestFor: Recruiters and community managers
Small businesses that sell through Instagram or Facebook
Anyone who wants replies to turn into follows
notes: The icons are 30 pixels, larger than the 22-pixel icons most templates use, which makes them easier to tap on a phone.

summary: A centred layout with the headshot on top, your name and role below, and a row of large social icons.
bestFor: Content creators and influencers
Coaches and speakers
Personal brands that live on social platforms
notes: Centred signatures look best when the email body is also short. In a long, left-aligned email it can feel detached from the text above it.

summary: A compact signature with a filled call-to-action button, such as Book a meeting, under your contact details.
bestFor: Sales reps who book demos
Consultants who take discovery calls
Anyone with one link they want clicked
notes: The button is a styled link rather than an image, so it still shows when images are blocked. Pro can also host an animated version of the button.

summary: Your details with a full-width call-to-action banner underneath, wider and more prominent than a button.
bestFor: Promotions, launches and events
Booking and enquiry links
Teams running a campaign through everyday email
notes: Change the banner text when the campaign changes. Old campaign wording is the most common reason signatures look out of date.

summary: A standard signature with a text link to your calendar under a brand-colour rule, rather than a button.
bestFor: People who share a Calendly or booking link
Account managers and customer success
A softer call to action than a button
notes: A text link is less pushy than a button and survives every email client, including ones that strip background colours.

summary: Headshot, stacked contact details and a filled button for a booking or listing link, with room for licence details below.
bestFor: Real estate agents and property managers
Mortgage brokers
Any role where the next step is a booking
notes: Turn on the compliance fields in the generator to add your licence number, brokerage and a standard disclaimer under the signature.

summary: A brand-colour bar beside your details, with labelled Call, Email and Web rows and the phone number first.
bestFor: Builders, electricians, plumbers and other trades
Field services and inspections
Businesses where customers phone rather than email
notes: Putting the phone number first and labelling it Call means a customer reading on a phone can tap it straight away.

summary: Your title in spaced capitals in your brand colour, an accent rule and a clean contact block.
bestFor: Consultants and advisers
Professional services firms
Specialists whose title carries weight
notes: The spaced-capital title reads as a credential, which suits roles where clients choose you for your expertise.

summary: Name, then title and company in small spaced capitals, an accent rule and stacked contact details.
bestFor: Design studios and architects
Boutique agencies
Hospitality and lifestyle brands
notes: The small capitals give an editorial, studio feel without needing a special font, since it uses the same email-safe fonts as every template.

summary: A bordered card with your details on the left, a call-to-action link on the right and social icons along the bottom.
bestFor: People who want a business-card look
Freelancers who share one key link
Signatures that need to stand apart from the message
notes: The border makes the signature read as a separate object, which helps when your emails are long or you often forward threads.

summary: A taller rectangular headshot beside a serif name and a spaced-capital title.
bestFor: Photographers and creative professionals
Authors and speakers
Anyone with a strong professional portrait
notes: This template needs a good photo. A low-resolution or busy headshot is more noticeable here than in the circular layouts.

summary: Your initials in a brand-colour circle instead of a photo, with your details beside it.
bestFor: People who do not want a headshot
New businesses without a logo yet
Shared team inboxes
notes: By default the monogram is text on a coloured circle, not an image, so it shows even when the recipient blocks images.

summary: A headshot with your details listed under small capital labels: phone, email and web.
bestFor: Roles with several ways to be contacted
Customer-facing support teams
People who like information laid out like a form
notes: The labels make it obvious which line is which, which helps readers who skim the signature looking for one detail.

summary: A headshot, a brand-colour accent and contact rows marked M, E and W in your brand colour.
bestFor: People who are mainly reached by mobile
Managers and team leads
A classic layout with a little more structure
notes: The single-letter markers are text in your brand colour, so they add structure without any extra images.

summary: A headshot, your name, your title with the company in your brand colour, then your contact lines.
bestFor: Firms that want to echo their printed letterhead
Accountants and advisers
People who send formal correspondence
notes: Highlighting the company name in brand colour keeps the business visible even when no logo is used.

summary: No photo: your name, title and company, a short rule, one contact line and small social icons.
bestFor: Developers and technical roles
Founders who want understatement
Anyone who finds most signatures too busy
notes: The short rule is the only decoration. It suits people who want a signature that does its job and gets out of the way.

summary: A tinted panel holding your headshot, details, a call-to-action button and social icons together.
bestFor: Founders and sales leaders
Event and launch periods
People who want every link in one tidy block
notes: The panel colour is set with the bgcolor attribute as well as CSS, so email clients that ignore CSS backgrounds still show the block.
